jsnvu6-e146211-d1e106.summary: Rubric heading for Question 1, stating the question to be treated: whether the power to sin is from God.
concepts: power to sin (potentia peccandi)
divine causality

jsnvu6-e146211-d1e113.summary: First objection: a power joined with act is more perfect than one separated from act; God is not the cause of the power to sin as joined with act, as already established at Distinction 37; therefore God is not its cause as separated from act either, and so in no way its cause.
claims: A power joined with act is more perfect than one separated from act
God is not the cause of the power to sin as joined with act (per Distinction 37)
Therefore God is not the cause of the power to sin in any sense
concepts: power joined with act versus separated from act
cross-reference to Distinction 37

jsnvu6-e146211-d1e129.summary: Second objection: if the power to sin were in us from God, it would have to be a natural power, a power of free choice, or a power of grace; but it cannot be purely natural, since such powers involve neither merit nor demerit; nor free choice, since per Anselm the ability to sin is neither liberty nor part of liberty; nor grace, since grace inclines toward the opposite of sin; therefore no power to sin is in us from God.
claims: The power to sin, if from God, would have to be natural, of free choice, or of grace
It is none of these three: not natural (no merit/demerit involved), not free choice (per Anselm, ability to sin is not liberty or part of it), not grace (which inclines away from sin)
Therefore the power to sin is not from God
concepts: threefold division of powers (natural, free choice, grace)
Anselm on liberty and the ability to sin

jsnvu6-e146211-d1e150.summary: Sed contra: Augustine states that the will is that by which one sins and by which one lives rightly; but the will is in us from God; therefore the power to sin is from God.
claims: Augustine holds that the will is the faculty by which one both sins and lives rightly
The will is in us from God
Therefore the power to sin is from God
concepts: Augustine on the will as common root of sin and right living

jsnvu6-e146211-d1e161.summary: Second sed contra: the Philosopher (Aristotle, in the Topics) says that the powers of evil things are good; every good is from God; therefore the power to sin or do evil is from God.
claims: Aristotle holds that the powers for evil things are themselves good
Every good is from God
Therefore the power to sin is from God
concepts: Aristotle on powers for evil as themselves good

jsnvu6-e146211-d1e172.summary: Responsio, presenting a first (reported) position. Since act determines the understanding of power—just as the act of sin includes both the act itself and a defect of due rectitude—so the power to sin signifies two things: the principle of act (insofar as it is a power) and the possibility of defect (that is, of sinning). On this basis, some hold that the power to sin, as to the first element (a nature principiating act), is from God, since whatever positively participates the nature of being must be traced to God as first cause, and this power, so considered, is the common principle of both ordered and disordered acts—hence, just as the power to act rightly is from God, so is the power to sin. But as to the second element, defectibility, it is not from God, directly or indirectly: supposing with Damascene that such defectibility belongs to a thing because it is from nothing, and that what belongs to a thing per se is not caused in it by another (at least not directly), while being from nothing belongs to the creature per se (since left to itself it is nothing), it follows that being-from-nothing is not from God directly; nor indirectly, since God is not the cause of any defect indirectly unless the thing is capable of the opposite perfection, and a creature is not capable of not being from nothing, that being the opposite belonging to it of itself.
claims: The power to sin has two elements: the natural principle of act (from God) and the defectibility or possibility of failure (allegedly not from God)

The reported position holds the defectibility of the power to sin is grounded in the creature's being 'from nothing,' which is proper to the creature per se and not caused in it by God, even indirectly
concepts: power to sin as principle-plus-defectibility
Damascene on creaturely defectibility from being ex nihilo
per se properties not caused by another

jsnvu6-e146211-d1e242.summary: Identifies a first flaw in the reported position: it wrongly assumes a creature has 'being from nothing' of itself. Recalling Distinction 1, a creature is not said to come to be or exist 'from nothing' materially, as subject, or as ordering term, but only negatively—coming to be from no presupposed substrate. This the creature has from God, not from itself: whatever is the cause of an affirmation is the cause of the negation that per se and immediately follows from it (e.g., what causes whiteness causes the corresponding non-blackness); God is the cause of the creature in everything that is in it, from which affirmation follows per se and immediately the negation that the creature does not come to be from any presupposed substrate—since were something presupposed, the whole would not be produced by God. Therefore God is the cause that the creature exists 'not from something'—which is the only sense in which it is said to be 'from nothing'—contrary to the reported position's assumption that this belongs to the creature of itself.
claims: The claim that a creature has 'being from nothing' of itself, not from God, is false

God, as total cause of the creature's affirmative being, is thereby also the cause of the correlative negation—that the creature presupposes no substrate—which is the only proper sense of 'being from nothing'
Hence 'being from nothing,' rightly understood, is itself from God, undermining the reported position's basis for denying God's causality of defectibility
concepts: cross-reference to Distinction 1 on 'ex nihilo'
affirmation and its immediate negation share a cause
creation without presupposed substrate

jsnvu6-e146211-d1e286.summary: Identifies a second flaw: the reasoning that a creature has 'being from nothing' of itself—because, left to itself, it would fall into nothing—actually proves the opposite. What is the effective and conserving cause of a thing's entity through its positive influence is thereby also the sufficient cause of that thing's non-entity through the mere withdrawal of that influence, as induction shows generally; God, through his influence, is the effective and conserving cause of the whole entity of any creature, so God alone, by withdrawing his influence, is the sufficient total cause of the creature's non-entity—no positive cause of the negative effect is needed, only the negative fact of God's not influencing. It is stranger still to say a creature 'of itself' is non-being or nothing, since the preposition 'from/of' denotes some kind of cause, and none applies here: not formal (the creature is formally a being, not nothing), not material (nothing, being total negation, can have no subject), not final (an end must have the character of being and good), not efficient (nothing has no efficient cause)—only a 'deficient' cause, which is the very same cause considered as withholding its efficiency toward being. Hence it belongs to a creature in no way of itself to be non-being or nothing; whether it exists or ceases to exist, the whole is from God, either influencing or withdrawing his influence. The reported position's first reason therefore proves nothing. Its second reason also assumes something false—that nothing causes a defect indirectly unless the subject is capable of the opposite perfection—since God, in causing a donkey at its proper grade of being, causes it to lack rationality even though the donkey is not capable of rationality; the same holds in the present case.
claims: The inference that a creature possesses non-being 'of itself' because it would fall into nothing if abandoned by God actually shows the opposite: God, as sole positive cause of the creature's being, is thereby the sole (negative) cause of its non-being

No causal sense (formal, material, final, or efficient) can support the claim that a creature is 'of itself' nothing or non-being; only a 'deficient' cause—God's withholding of influence—accounts for it
The premise that a defect requires capacity for the opposite perfection to be indirectly caused is false, as the case of the naturally non-rational donkey shows
concepts: conserving cause as sufficient cause of non-being upon withdrawal
the preposition 'ex/de nihilo' analyzed by the four causes
deficient causality
counterexample from natural species limitation

jsnvu6-e146211-d1e360.summary: Identifies a further flaw, concerning the claim (following Damascene) that a creature's being from nothing entails a double revertibility into nothing—of natural being (were it totally annihilated) and of choice (since, per Augustine, sin is nothing, so sinning reverts the sinner's choice into nothing). While the first revertibility (of total entity) is adequately explained by the creature's dependence on God's conserving influence, it is not evident that the same source explains revertibility of choice into sin, since creatures also undergo other reversions not attributed to being ex nihilo—a man's sight reverting to blindness, or any corporeal thing's being reverting to non-being through corruption (without total annihilation)—all of which are equally reversions 'from habit into privation,' like sin. If the same reasoning applied uniformly, every such mutability would have to be attributed to the creature's being from nothing, which is not commonly held.
claims: The claim that revertibility of choice into sin follows from the creature's being 'ex nihilo,' in the same way total annihilability does, is unproven
Other creaturely reversions from habit into privation (blindness, corruption) are structurally parallel to sin but are not commonly attributed to being ex nihilo, undermining the uniform explanation
concepts: Damascene's double revertibility into nothing
sin as privation (per Augustine)
reversion from habit to privation as a general pattern

jsnvu6-e146211-d1e422.summary: Argues further: if being-from-nothing were the cause of all revertibilities from habit into privation, it would be either an immediate/proximate or a remote/mediate cause. It cannot be immediate, since a sufficient immediate cause entails its effect, yet being-from-nothing belongs equally to every creature, so all revertibilities would then belong equally to every creature—which is false, since some creatures (heaven, separated substances) lack revertibility to corruption, and some (irrational creatures) lack revertibility of choice. If it is instead a remote, mediate cause, it cannot sufficiently account for the specific revertibilities in question. Therefore it is said quite insufficiently that the defectibility of choice belongs to a creature because it is from nothing.
claims: Being-from-nothing cannot be the immediate cause of all revertibilities, since it belongs equally to all creatures while the revertibilities themselves vary by kind of creature
Nor can it be a sufficient remote cause, since a remote cause cannot adequately explain the specific revertibility in question
The explanation of defectibility of choice via being-from-nothing is therefore insufficient
concepts: immediate versus remote/mediate causation
variation of revertibility across kinds of creature

jsnvu6-e146211-d1e461.summary: Identifies a third flaw, bearing on the main conclusion itself: it is false that the defectibility of the power to sin is not from God. A defect lacking the character of evil can be caused by God at least as readily as one that has the character of evil; but defects having the character of evil are caused by God (the evil of punishment is from God, per Distinction 37); therefore a fortiori, a defect lacking the character of evil is from God. Such a defect is the mere possibility of failing in choosing, which is neither fault (else man would always sin) nor punishment (since it existed in the state of innocence, where nothing was penal), but a pure limitation of created intellectual nature, which cannot attain the perfection of uncreated nature (in which no defect of knowing or choosing is possible)—yet this limitation is not itself evil, since it removes no perfection due to the creature; hence it is from God. Further, the same judgment should apply to every possibility of failing, whether from God or not; and it is certain that the possibility of failing through corruption is from God in corporeal creatures, since the universal order—intended per se by God—requires that some things be able to fail and sometimes do fail (plants nourishing animals, animals and plants nourishing humans, per Genesis 1 and 9), the corruption of one thereby serving the conservation of another; by the same reasoning, the possibility of failing in choosing is likewise from God.
claims: A defect without the character of evil (like the mere possibility of failing in choice) is, a fortiori, caused by God, since even defects with the character of evil (punishment) are caused by God
The possibility of failing in choice is a pure limitation of created intellectual nature—neither fault nor punishment—and so is compatible with being from God
By analogy with the possibility of corruption in corporeal creatures (required by the universal order, per Genesis), the possibility of failing in choosing is likewise from God
concepts: defect without evil versus defect with evil (punishment)
limitation of created versus uncreated intellectual nature
universal order requiring the possibility of failure (Genesis 1 and 9)

jsnvu6-e146211-d1e524.summary: Reply to the first argument (d1e113): among good things, a power joined with act is indeed more perfect than one separated from act, but among evil things it is less perfect, since evil itself is a kind of imperfection; if it is called 'more perfect' in the evil case, this is only by a transferred use of the term, as 'perfect' is figuratively applied to evils (per Metaphysics V)—so the major premise is false. The minor is also false: it was not said at Distinction 37 that God is not the cause of the power to sin as joined with act, but only that he is not the immediate cause of the evil act itself, and therefore that act cannot be imputed to him as fault.
claims: The objection's major premise fails: a power joined with act is more perfect only among good things; among evil things the reverse holds, and 'more perfect' is applied to evil only figuratively
The objection's minor premise misreads Distinction 37, which denied only that God is the immediate cause of the evil act, not that he is the cause of the power to sin as joined with act
concepts: reply to objection
figurative use of 'perfect' applied to evil
clarification of Distinction 37's claim

jsnvu6-e146211-d1e548.summary: Reply to the second argument (d1e129): the power to sin is the power of free choice. As for Anselm's statement that the ability to sin is neither liberty nor part of liberty, Anselm means only that the ability to sin is not essential to liberty as such—otherwise God, who cannot sin, would not have free choice—not that the power of free choice in creatures lacks the ability to sin, or that the ability to sin is incompatible with liberty.
claims: The power to sin is identified with the power of free choice

Anselm's dictum means only that the ability to sin is not essential to liberty as such (since God, unable to sin, is nonetheless free), not that creaturely free choice lacks or excludes the ability to sin
concepts: reply to objection
Anselm's dictum on liberty and the ability to sin, correctly construed
God's freedom despite impeccability

jsnvu6-e146211.summary: Question 1 asks whether the power to sin is from God. Two objections deny it (a power joined with act is more perfect than separated, yet God is not the cause of the power to sin as joined with act per Distinction 37; and the power to sin cannot be natural, free choice, or grace, per Anselm), while two sed contra arguments affirm it, from Augustine (the will, which is from God, is that by which one both sins and lives rightly) and Aristotle (powers for evil things are themselves good, and all good is from God). The responsio first reports a distinguishing position: the power to sin has a natural-principle element (from God) and a defectibility element (allegedly not from God, being grounded instead in the creature's being 'from nothing'). This reported position is then subjected to sustained critique across several flaws: the notion that a creature has 'being from nothing' of itself, rather than from God, is refuted by showing God causes both the creature's affirmative being and its correlative negation; the inference from creaturely fragility to a distinct non-divine source of defectibility is shown to prove the opposite, since God's conserving causality is itself sufficient (by withdrawal) to explain non-being; the attempt to derive defectibility of choice specifically from being-from-nothing is shown to be unmotivated, since analogous creaturely reversions (blindness, corruption) are not so explained, and being-from-nothing cannot function as either an adequate immediate or remote cause of the variable revertibilities found across different kinds of creature; and, addressing the main conclusion directly, the defectibility of choice—being a defect without the character of evil—is shown, a fortiori and by analogy with the God-caused possibility of corruption required by the universal order, to be from God as well. The replies to the opening objections then clarify that 'more perfect' applies to power-joined-with-act only among goods, not evils, and that Distinction 37 denied only God's immediate causality of the evil act itself, not of the power to sin; and that Anselm's dictum denies only that the ability to sin is essential to liberty, not that it is compatible with (created) freedom.
claims: The power to sin, in both its natural-principial aspect and its defectibility aspect, is from God as first cause

The creature's 'being from nothing' does not name a source of defectibility independent of God; rightly understood, it is itself grounded in God's causality (as the negation immediately following his positive causing of the creature)
God's causing an evil act via the power he grants is distinct from his being the immediate cause of that act's evil character, which is not imputed to him

The possibility of failing in choice, being a defect without the character of evil, is required by the same divine ordering of the universe that permits corruption among corporeal creatures, and is therefore from God
concepts: divine causality of the power to sin
defectibility and being ex nihilo
deficient causality
limitation of created versus uncreated nature
free choice and the ability to sin (Anselm)
